sections.title: What the study says actually helped

toc.title: Departure three: "Polyvagal Theory is just a theory too"

blocks.p: In episode 149, I laid out the case that you don't have parts, you don't have a shadow self, you don't have an ego, and no, not even a puzzle self. These are metaphors that can be helpful, but I don't think they're real things. That's the basic idea. Here I want to go deeper and respond to some of the rebuttals I got. My hope is that you get your ideas challenged in a playful and stimulating, but yes, challenging way, and maybe gain some more clarity, or at least something fun to think about.

I do appreciate the rebuttals and the disagreements. Everyone was super cool about it, so I'm going to try to match your energy and be tactful. But I'm finding the more I talk about this, the more strongly I actually feel about it. Or maybe one of my parts does. That's a joke. We've got to start off a little bit light. Grab my hand, let's go.

For the most part, I don't disagree with people. I think we're pretty much on the same page with a lot of this. But there are points where I depart from you, and that's what I want to make clear. I'm going to focus on IFS (Internal Family Systems) a bit more here, because that's mostly what the objections were about.

blocks.h: I was wrong: they mean it literally

blocks.p: The first thing I have to address is that I was wrong about something. I thought that parts in particular, but also the shadow stuff and the ego stuff, were known to be metaphors. I thought we were all in on this.

Then I went to the IFS website. In an article called "Internal Family Systems Model Outline," it says: "It is the nature of the mind to be subdivided into an indeterminate number of subpersonalities or parts."

How they know that, I have no idea. They're assuming it. They're asserting it. They're saying this is how things are, with no evidence. In the realm of people entrusting their mental health to you, philosophically and scientifically, that cannot be good enough, in my opinion. Same thing with Freud and all of his ideas. Same thing with the shadow stuff. We cannot just say, "Here, this is the truth," without evidence.

If they had just said, "These are metaphors, and we want you to use this metaphor as a way to get to your truer experience," I'd have no problem with that. There's a level of equality there. When I say, "Hey, I have this idea. It's a metaphor I want to use in my therapy. Are you on the same page?" you can say yes or no. We both know it's a metaphor. We know it's made up, and that's okay. There's a lot of utility to metaphors and using your imagination.

But when you say, "I know the truth about reality, and reality is that you have parts to your personality," without defining what a subpersonality is, without defining what the nature of the mind is, that becomes something else. That's not a person offering an idea. That's a person on a mountain who comes back and says, "I have the truth, and I'm bestowing it upon you through my workbook and my course."

blocks.h: This is a psychology problem, not just an IFS problem

blocks.p: To be fair, this is not just an IFS issue. It's a psychology issue. We are terrible at explaining what we mean. Ask any therapist, any psychologist, anybody really, "What is the mind? What is consciousness?" and you'll get a different answer from each of them, because we're terrible at defining things. We just sort of run with it.
I'm guilty of that too. I'm working on my understanding of what these things could mean. I'm part of the problem, and I have to admit that.

IFS goes beyond that, though. It asserts not only that the mind is something, but that they know the true nature of the mind, and that it involves parts or subpersonalities. They also say everyone has a self, and the self can and should lead the individual's internal system. They're not calling that a metaphor either. They mean it literally. That's a whole different level of claim, and it requires some evidence, not just theorizing and playing around with ideas.

blocks.h: Departure one: yes, it adds a cognitive layer

blocks.p: One of the big rebuttals was: "No, it doesn't add a cognitive layer. It actually adds an experiential layer."

I agree to some extent. These things can lead to a new experience, a more direct felt experience. But to get there, you have to go through the cognitions, what I call metaphors: the shadow, the ego, the parts. You have to believe them first. With IFS, you have to believe specifically what IFS is saying, because they're saying, "This is the truth." You can believe that with them, and that's fine. But that is a belief, and that's a big cognitive layer.

That's different, in my opinion, from learning about the Polyvagal Theory, or learning how to name and describe your internal sensations. Yes, you're learning something new there too, but it's way more direct, and it's grounded in reality.

And it's not just one layer. IFS tells you that, rather than going directly to the experience, you first have to learn and believe that you have parts, that those parts have their own wants, and that those parts interact with each other. Here's what the IFS website says about firefighters.

First: "Firefighters are a group of parts that react when exiles are activated in an effort to control and extinguish their feelings." A group of parts, not a part. That was new to me. Just from that one sentence, here are the layers you'd have to believe in order to get to your felt sense:

ul: The concept of parts, and not just as a concept but declared as reality.
The concept of groups of parts.
Parts reacting to other parts' reactions.

blocks.p: So they interact with each other, they have feelings, they have desires, they have thoughts. Do you see the numerous layers you'd have to understand to get where you want to go? Hopefully you get there.

Second, firefighters have the same goal as managers, which is to keep exiles away, but different strategies. From this we learn that these parts can strategize. That means they can think, look to the future, and put together a coordinated set of behaviors to get their own goals met. Lots of questions come up, but I'll leave it at that.
Third, firefighters can do this in any number of ways, including, in their words, "drug or alcohol use, self-mutilation or cutting, binge eating, and sex binges."

I read that and I say, they're talking about behavioral adaptations. That's what we'd call it through the lens of the Polyvagal Theory. Anybody else would say you're coping, and maybe these aren't the healthiest coping behaviors, but they're coping behaviors. Two words: coping behaviors. Or another two words: behavioral adaptations.

As far as I can understand it, what they're saying is that firefighters implement ways to reduce emotional dysregulation. In polyvagal terms, you're doing things to reduce autonomic dysregulation. You don't need the firefighters. If you're a therapist, you can just say to your client, "So you're doing these things to alleviate your own distress."

That's a hell of a lot simpler than saying that your firefighter parts group is reacting to your exile parts group being activated, trying to control or extinguish their feelings through a strategy like cutting, and that your manager parts group has the same goal but different strategies.
Rather than all that, I'd just say, "So you cut in order to get some relief." And my clients do this weird thing where they say, "Yeah," and that's it.
I know I sound arrogant. This is how I sound. But do you see the difference? That's cognitive layering that is wildly unnecessary, in my opinion.

I said this in episode 149, but these added layers are not necessary. I don't do this stuff at all in the way I work. If anything, it clouds the issue. It makes it harder to get to the direct experience. We don't have to go through these cognitive layers to get there.

I fully believe metaphors and imagination are very useful. I use them a lot. I just don't use these ones. And when I do use a metaphor, I make it very clear: "Let's just play pretend. Let's use our imagination." Then I use some image that's relevant to that client. Usually they come up with it themselves, and I encourage it: "Let's stick with that. Let's play with that." I don't tell them what they should think before they get to their direct experience.

When you assert that this is how the world is, that requires belief. When it's a metaphor, you don't have to believe anything. You can just join in. Take puzzle self therapy, my made-up example from episode 149. It's not real. But I could say, "Hey, I have a metaphor. Do you want to join me?" and you could say yes. If I say, "No, you really do have a puzzle inside of you, in reality," and you say, "You're right, I do," now you're believing me. That's different.

blocks.h: Departure two: does it build internal awareness?

blocks.p: The next rebuttal was that this approach helps build internal insight and felt experience. For you, I don't doubt that it can. I don't think you need the cognitive layers about parts to get there.

I looked at one of the studies from IFS's own website. One of its conclusions says: "Change on most indicators of interoceptive awareness were not significant, with the exception of a small but significant change in ability to refrain from using distraction or ignoring to cope with sensations of pain and discomfort."

So the thing people like about this model is that it helps them look inward and build more access to their felt sense. If you get that, awesome. I'm happy for you. But according to one of their own studies, it mostly didn't do that.

blocks.h3: What the study says actually helped

blocks.p: The study did have promising results, and it listed why. I respect that they put all this in. They should be transparent, and I appreciated it. I'm not saying they're dishonest. Here's what it gave as reasons its results were stronger than other studies on PTSD symptoms:

ul: It was an open, uncontrolled trial. It wasn't randomized and wasn't comparing IFS to anything else within the trial. That's not ideal.
Women tend to have a stronger response to PTSD treatment, and this study was 76% women.

There was a lot of therapy: sixteen 90-minute sessions, which is higher than typical PTSD treatment, and the study acknowledges that. People who benefit from treatment early tend to stay in treatment longer, and the benefits accumulate.
The number of trauma-focused sessions has been shown to predict results, and IFS addresses trauma right away and consistently.

blocks.p: None of that has to do with parts.

I'll go one step further. The conclusion says IFS may provide an alternative to interventions using cognitive and exposure-based methods, in that it utilizes a comprehensive, mindful, and compassion-based approach. Not because of parts work. Not because of viewing things as parts. They didn't control for the parts work, by the way. They didn't isolate it as a variable, and I think that's an issue with a lot of studies.
So by their own words, what's helpful is a comprehensive, mindful, compassion-based approach. Of course that helps. You don't need the parts metaphor for that to work.

blocks.h: Departure three: "Polyvagal Theory is just a theory too"

blocks.p: A couple of people pointed out that in episode 149 I said there's no blood test for shadows, and answered, "Well, there's no blood test for attachment or Polyvagal Theory either. They're all just theories."

No, not really. These are wildly different. The Polyvagal Theory is science. It's not a declaration. There are hundreds of peer-reviewed articles. Porges has his own lab where he studies heart rate variability and how it relates to the vagus nerve.

There's also criticism of the Polyvagal Theory, and that's part of science. That's a good thing. Grossman is a serious critic, and Porges has responded to him. That's the norm for science, because ultimately what Porges puts out can be wrong. It can be disputed. Somebody can come along and say, "You've got it wrong. I have new evidence." There are hypotheses, and there's an element of falsifiability.

That's not true for Internal Family Systems or shadow work or ego. All I can do is make a logical argument against them and ask for evidence: "Show me the parts. Do something to indicate this is real." Yes, I'm offering an alternative and flat out negating this stuff, but the burden is not on me to disprove it. The burden is on the people making it up to prove it.

The same goes for attachment. Porges' wife, Sue Carter, does research on love and connection and how oxytocin and vasopressin are part of it. She's not simply declaring something. She's doing research that can be falsified and saying, "Here are my results." That's way different from going into a different room for ten minutes, thinking, and coming back to say, "I've got it." And if you want to equate all of these things, then puzzle self therapy is in the mix too. You've opened the door for all kinds of nonsense.
One last thing. There's a problem when a critique somehow gets turned into proof. When I say, "I don't believe in this stuff," and I'm told, "That's one of your parts talking," no. That's me.

I don't believe the primary assertion that we have parts. I don't believe we have a shadow self. Metaphorically, these are fine. I don't care. But when you're talking about objective reality, I don't believe you. So if you notice yourself taking someone's disagreement and filtering it into "this actually proves my case," I'd really encourage you to question that. Does it? No, of course not.
If this is an issue for you, I may have lost you as a listener, and I'm sad to think that. You're absolutely invited to keep coming back.

My goal is to challenge ideas out there that I think need to be challenged. I also have to acknowledge that I'm making an argument. I'm trying to convince you of something. If I've failed, I'm okay with that, and I respect whatever thoughts you have. But I think disagreeing, putting it out there, and inviting more disagreement is fun, interesting, and a necessary part of rational thought. That's how we build on the ideas that are rational and helpful and make sense compared to the objective world, and let go of the ones that aren't necessary.
The mental health field is very special to me, and it needs an overhaul. I don't mean that in a joking way. There are some major issues in psychology and in the practice of therapy.
So thank you to everyone who responded, even the person who called me arrogant. For the most part, I agree with you. What I've highlighted here are the places where we diverge.
